transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I’m Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

Hi, Dr. [Your Name]. Um, well, I came in because... I just keep getting stuck on this tiny uneven spot around my nose and my cheek. Especially in photos, or like, under those awful fluorescent lights at the store where I work. I'm a cashier, and honestly, the lighting there is just the worst. It makes everything look so harsh. The other day, this lady came through my line with like, three carts full of groceries, and I swear she was just staring at me the whole time I was scanning her items. It took forever because the barcode on the frozen peas wouldn't scan. I hate when that happens, it holds up the whole line and everyone gets so impatient. But anyway, even when other people tell me they don't see the spot, it just feels like it's the very first thing all the customers and my managers notice about me.
How much time do you spend each day thinking about that uneven spot on your face, and does it interfere with your work or other activities?

Um, how much time? I don't know, a lot, I guess. It's always sort of there in the back of my mind. Like, on my breaks at work, instead of actually relaxing or eating my lunch—which I usually just bring a sandwich anyway, turkey and Swiss, but the deli meat has been so expensive lately, have you noticed that? It's like five dollars just for a tiny little pack now. But anyway, instead of eating, I end up going to the bathroom and just checking my face in the mirror. 

I try to fix my hair so it sort of falls around that side of my nose and cheek to cover it up. And I can't help but compare myself to the girls who come through my line. Some of them just have this perfect, smooth skin, and they're buying all this expensive makeup, which reminds me, our store stopped carrying my favorite concealer and I had to drive all the way to the mall to find it last week. Traffic was a nightmare. But yeah, sometimes I get so caught up checking the mirror and trying to fix my hair that I lose track of time, and I end up being late getting back to the register. My manager gets so annoyed when I do that.
Do you believe that this uneven spot on your face is an actual physical defect, or do you worry that others might think it's a defect even if it's not obvious to them?

Well, I mean... I know other people say they don't see it. My mom always tells me I'm making a big deal out of nothing, but moms kind of have to say that stuff, right? She actually just got this brand new phone, one of those ones with like three different cameras on the back, and the picture quality is just insane. She took a picture of my cat, Mittens, the other day and you could literally see every single little whisker. Mittens is getting so old, though, we've had him since I was in like, sixth grade. He sleeps all day on the radiator now. 

But anyway, when she takes pictures of me with that phone, or like I was saying before, when I'm under those terrible store lights, I just know it's a real thing. I get so stuck on that tiny uneven spot on my cheek and nose because I can clearly see it. So even if other people claim it's not obvious, to me it's a real physical thing on my face. It just feels like it's the absolute first thing all the customers and my managers are staring at. Especially my manager, Dave. He always stands way too close when he's doing till checks, and he breathes so loud, it's super distracting. But yeah, I really do think it's an actual spot that everyone is noticing, even if they pretend they aren't.

latest_inference.note: The patient's belief that the facial irregularity is a real and noticeable defect, despite reassurance from others, along with preoccupation and repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, grooming), supports Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.22). Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1) and Major Depressive Disorder, Mild (F32.0) remain less likely given the specific focus of concern and behaviors, though further evaluation may be needed.

candidates: F32.0 Major depressive disorder, single episode, mild
inference_history.note: The patient presents with preoccupation about a perceived physical defect (uneven spot on face), significant distress related to appearance, and avoidance behaviors in social contexts (e.g., concern about being judged by customers and managers), which suggests possible body dysmorphic disorder. There is also evidence of social anxiety and potential depressive features, which are included in the differential. No information yet to rule out any of these conditions.
